questions.q: A school model of matter in Kanada's scheme is built with bead groups: 5 dyads and 4 triads. How many parmanus (single beads) does the whole model need?
questions.a: 22. A dyad has 2 parmanus and a triad has 3, so 5 x 2 + 4 x 3 = 10 + 12 = 22; 9 counts groups, not parmanus.

questions.q: A chemistry student wants to use Kanada's idea to predict how much of each kind of parmanu must be combined to make a given substance. What stops her, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter notes that Kanada's description does not specify the proportions in which parmanus combine, so no quantity can be predicted from it.
o: The description does not specify the proportions in which parmanus combine to form different substances
Parmanus can be divided further, so no counting is possible
Kanada's text was written after Dalton's atomic theory
Dyads are formed only from three parmanus

questions.q: A quiz sheet asks for a pairing of each thinker with the basis of his idea of an indivisible particle. Which pairing matches the chapter?
questions.a: The earliest atom ideas of Kanada and the Greeks were imaginary ideas, not experimental; Dalton's 1808 theory rested on experiments of his time.
o: Leucippus and Democritus: imagined by reasoning; Dalton: based on scientific experiments of his time
Leucippus and Democritus: based on experiments; Dalton: imagined by reasoning
Kanada: based on experiments; Dalton: imagined by reasoning
Kanada and Dalton: both based on experiments of their time

questions.q: Dalton's atoms were described as fundamental building blocks 'that cannot be broken down into smaller parts'. The chapter says that scientists later found a reason to doubt this. Which finding is it?
questions.a: Radiation from certain elements (radioactivity) showed that atoms are composed of smaller particles, so they were not indivisible as previously believed.
o: Certain elements emit radiation, which showed atoms must contain smaller particles
Atoms of different elements were found to have the same colour
The Greek word atomos was found to mean 'divisible'
Kanada's text was found to describe dyads of atoms

questions.q:
Read the statements about early ideas of the atom.
Statement 1: Kanada said a parmanu can be seen clearly through a strong lens.
Statement 2: A dyad is a group of two parmanus and a triad is a group of three.
Statement 3: Dalton's atomic theory was based on scientific experiments of that time.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: A parmanu cannot be perceived by the senses, so statement 1 is false. Statements 2 and 3 agree with the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dalton's atomic theory is called the first scientific description of how matter is made.
Reason (R): The Greek philosophers Leucippus and Democritus called indivisible particles atomos.
questions.a: A is true because Dalton's theory rested on experiments. R is also true, but the Greek idea was imagined, not experimental, so R does not explain why Dalton's theory is called scientific.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A body in Kanada's scheme is built from 6 dyads. The number of parmanus in it is ___.

Match each description in column I with the term in column II.
Column I: 1. The Sanskrit name for what remains when matter is divided again and again until division stops  2. A group made when three parmanus join  3. The word, meaning indivisible, used by Leucippus and Democritus  4. The first description of matter's structure that rested on experiments, proposed in 1808
Column II: a. triad  b. atomos  c. parmanu  d. Dalton's atomic theory
questions.a: Parmanu is the smallest particle; three joined make a triad; atomos is the Greek word; the 1808 experiment-based theory is Dalton's.

questions.q: True or False: Since Kanada in India and Democritus in Greece both imagined indivisible particles, their ideas count as scientific atomic theories, just like Dalton's. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Both ideas were imaginary or philosophical ideas, not based on experimental observations; only Dalton's 1808 theory was based on scientific experiments.
s: Correction: earlier ideas were imaginary, only Dalton's rested on experiments

questions.q:
A group of 12 parmanus is made only of triads.
(a) How many triads are there?
(b) If the same 12 parmanus are regrouped into dyads only, how many more groups are there than before?
questions.a: (a) 12 / 3 = 4 triads. (b) 12 / 2 = 6 dyads, which is 6 - 4 = 2 more groups.

questions.q:
(a) State the basis on which the idea of the atom first arose, according to the chapter.
(b) Using your answer to (a), explain why the chapter calls Dalton's theory 'the first scientific description' of matter.
questions.a: (a) It originated as an imaginary idea, not from experimental observations. (b) Dalton's theory was the first to be based on scientific experiments of his time, so it was the first scientific description.
s: Part (b): Dalton's rested on experiments, so first scientific

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why Kanada's claim about parmanus could not have been tested by an experiment in his time.
questions.a: A parmanu is infinitely small and cannot be perceived by the senses, and his description does not give the proportions in which parmanus combine, so no measurable prediction follows.
s: Reason 1: cannot be perceived by the senses

questions.q: A student says, 'Dalton's atoms were indivisible, and the electron was found in 1897, so Dalton must have been proved wrong in every respect.' Is this fully right? Explain in two points.
questions.a: Partly. The idea that atoms cannot be divided was later given up, but Dalton's theory was still the first scientific description and became the starting point for the current understanding of atomic structure.
s: Verdict: partly right; indivisibility given up
Still the starting point of atomic structure

questions.q: After Dalton's theory, scientists asked what atoms are made up of. Do you think this question could have been answered by reasoning alone, as Kanada's was? Give one reason.
questions.a: No. Dalton's theory was based on experiments, so the next question about what atoms are made of needed new experiments and evidence, such as the cathode ray and gold foil experiments, not reasoning alone.
s: Reason linked to Dalton's experimental basis

questions.q: Rohit says, 'Kanada in India and Democritus in Greece reached the same idea independently, so both of them proved that atoms exist.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The two civilisations did pose the same question and proposed a similar idea of indivisible particles. But the idea was imaginary and not based on experiments, so it did not prove that atoms exist.
s: Credits the parallel idea (parmanu and atomos)

questions.q: Show that a body of exactly 7 parmanus cannot be formed from dyads alone, and show that a mixture of dyads and triads can form it.
questions.a: Dyads have 2 parmanus each, so any number of dyads gives an even total; 7 is odd, so it cannot be made. With dyads and triads, 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 (two dyads and one triad) works.

questions.q: Design two different bead-models for a body of 20 parmanus, each using at least one dyad and at least one triad. State the number of dyads and triads in each and check the total.
questions.a: Any two of: 7 dyads and 2 triads (14 + 6 = 20); 4 dyads and 4 triads (8 + 12 = 20); 1 dyad and 6 triads (2 + 18 = 20).

questions.q: Trace the idea of the atom in five steps, with one line on each: (i) Kanada, (ii) Leucippus and Democritus, (iii) Dalton, (iv) what the discovery of radiation showed, (v) what scientists asked after Dalton.
questions.a: (i) Kanada: parmanus that cannot be divided further, forming dyads and triads. (ii) Leucippus and Democritus: atomos, indivisible particles. (iii) Dalton (1808): atoms as indivisible building blocks, based on experiments. (iv) Radiation showed atoms are made of smaller particles, so not indivisible. (v) Scientists asked what atoms are made of, what they look like, and what makes the atoms of one element different from another's.

questions.q: A friend says, 'Ideas with no experiments behind them are useless in science.' Using Kanada, the Greeks and Dalton, write a balanced reply: give two points for the friend's view, two points against it, and your own conclusion.
questions.a: For: Kanada's and the Greek ideas were imaginary and could not be tested, and Kanada gave no proportions. Against: they asked the same fundamental question 'what is everything made up of?' and gave a similar answer, and Dalton's experiment-based theory then became the starting point. Conclusion: a reasoned view, such as imaginative ideas are valuable as starting points but science needs experiments to confirm them.
s: Uses Dalton as the experimental follow-up

questions.q:
A school in Pune builds a bead model of Kanada's idea for its science exhibition. Group A makes a body from 9 triads and 6 dyads. Group B wants a 31-bead body using dyads only.
(a) How many beads does Group A's body use?
(b) Show whether Group B's plan can work.
(c) What does Kanada's description leave out that a visitor might ask about when seeing Group A's model?
(d) The panel has space for only one more item: the bead model with a note on Kanada, or a poster on Dalton's experiment-based theory. Choose one and say what the visitors lose.
questions.a: (a) 9 x 3 + 6 x 2 = 27 + 12 = 39 beads. (b) Dyads give an even total and 31 is odd, so it cannot work with dyads only. (c) The proportions in which parmanus combine to form different substances. (d) Either choice with a loss named: the bead model shows the ancient imaginary idea but not how matter was studied by experiment; the Dalton poster shows the first scientific description but not where the question began.
s: Part (b): 31 is odd, dyads give even totals
Part (d): a choice with the loss named

questions.q:
Aditi drafts a school-magazine article on atoms with four sentences: (1) Kanada said a parmanu can be seen with a lens. (2) Leucippus and Democritus named the indivisible particle atomos. (3) Dalton's 1808 theory was based on experiments. (4) Dalton's theory is many centuries older than Kanada's.
(a) Which two sentences are wrong, and how should each be corrected?
(b) What does the chapter mean by calling the early atom an 'imaginary idea'?
(c) Name two questions the chapter says scientists asked after Dalton.
(d) The editor must choose a headline: 'Dalton discovered the atom' or 'Dalton gave the atom its first scientific description'. Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) Sentence 1: a parmanu cannot be perceived by the senses. Sentence 4: Dalton's theory came many centuries after Kanada's. (b) The idea arose by thought, not from experimental observations. (c) Any two of: what atoms are made up of; what they would look like; what makes the atoms of one element different from another's. (d) The second headline is more accurate, because the idea of an indivisible particle existed earlier; Dalton's contribution was the first experiment-based description. The first headline is shorter but overclaims.
s: Part (b): arose by thought, not experiment

questions.q: Meena makes a Thomson-style atom: a clay ball standing for +9 units of positive charge, with 10 beads each standing for -1 unit pressed into it. What does her model show?
questions.a: Net charge = +9 - 10 = -1, so the model is not neutral; a neutral atom needs total positive charge equal to total negative charge.
o: A model with a net charge of -1, so it does not represent a neutral atom
A neutral atom, since positive and negative charges are present
A model with a net charge of +1, because clay is heavier
A neutral atom, since 10 beads are more than 9 units

questions.q: Ravi repeats Thomson's tube experiment with a copper cathode in hydrogen gas, then an iron cathode in air, at very low pressure and high voltage. The rays behave the same way each time. What does Ravi conclude?
questions.a: Because the nature of cathode rays was independent of the cathode material and the gas, electrons are a fundamental component of all atoms, present in every element.
o: The rays are negative particles that are a fundamental component of the atoms of every element
The rays come only from the gas atoms and never from the metal atoms
The rays are positive particles whose mass depends on the metal used
The rays are made only by copper and iron, which are metals

questions.q: In the gold foil experiment the chapter calls an alpha particle 'a nucleus of a helium atom containing two protons and two neutrons'. Taking the proton's relative charge as +1 and the neutron's as 0, what is the relative charge of an alpha particle?
questions.a: +2. Only the two protons contribute charge; the two neutrons add none, so it is not +4.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of Thomson's model of the atom?
questions.a: A tiny dense centre of positive charge belongs to Rutherford's nucleus; Thomson spread the positive charge through the whole sphere.
o: The positive charge is gathered in a tiny dense centre
The atom is a sphere of positive charge
Electrons are distributed throughout the positive sphere
The charges in the atom balance, so the atom is neutral

questions.q:
Read the statements about Thomson's experiment.
Statement 1: Cathode rays moved from the cathode (negative electrode) to the anode (positive electrode).
Statement 2: The nature of the rays changed whenever the cathode material was changed.
Statement 3: The rays were streams of negatively charged particles with a much smaller mass than atoms.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: The rays were independent of cathode material and gas, so statement 2 is false; statements 1 and 3 match the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A few alpha particles bounced back when fired at thin gold foil.
Reason (R): The positive charge in a gold atom is spread out evenly through the atom.
questions.a: A is true: some particles bounced back. R is false: Thomson's evenly spread charge could not cause a bounce back; the positive charge is concentrated in a nucleus.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: In a Thomson-model atom the positive sphere carries +17 units of charge. For the atom to be neutral, it must have ___ electrons, each of charge -1.

Match each observation or picture in column I with the idea it points to in column II.
Column I: 1. Nearly all alpha particles pass straight through the foil  2. A few alpha particles return the way they came  3. Rays seen travelling from the negative to the positive electrode in a low-pressure tube  4. Seeds scattered through the red pulp of a watermelon
Column II: a. Electrons distributed through a positive sphere  b. Cathode rays  c. Most of the atom is empty space  d. Positive charge concentrated in a tiny region
questions.a: Straight passage points to empty space, bounce back to a tiny concentrated positive region, the tube rays are cathode rays, and the watermelon picture is Thomson's plum pudding model.

questions.q: True or False: Because most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, Rutherford concluded that the atoms of gold have no positive charge. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Most particles passing through shows that most of the atom is empty space; the few sharp deflections and bounce backs show that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
s: Correction: positive charge exists but is concentrated in a nucleus

questions.q:
One alpha particle passes through the gold foil undeflected; another bounces back.
(a) What does the first suggest about the part of the atom it crossed?
(b) What does the second suggest about what it met?
questions.a: (a) It crossed empty space, since most of the atom is empty. (b) It met a tiny, concentrated region of positive charge that sharply deflected or reflected it.

questions.q:
(a) In Thomson's tube, between which two electrodes did the rays move, and in which direction?
(b) The rays were also found to have a much smaller mass than atoms. What did this suggest about atoms?
questions.a: (a) From the cathode (negative) to the anode (positive). (b) Since such particles were emitted from atoms, atoms are composed of smaller subatomic components.

questions.q: Could an orange, with seeds inside soft pulp, be as good a comparison for Thomson's atom as the watermelon? Give one way it matches and one way it falls short.
questions.a: It matches because the seeds sit scattered in the soft pulp, like electrons in the positive sphere. It falls short, for example, because the pulp does not represent positive charge balancing the seeds' charge, and an orange has a rind and segments that an atom model does not have.

questions.q: State the two features of the gold foil results that the chapter says Thomson's model failed to explain.
questions.a: The deflection of some alpha particles through large angles, and the fact that most of the alpha particles passed undeflected.

questions.q: A student asks why a single alpha particle bouncing back is enough to rule out the plum pudding model, when thousands passed through. Answer in two points.
questions.a: In Thomson's model the positive charge is spread evenly, so the positive alpha particle should be at most slightly deflected and never thrown back. A bounce back needs a strongly repelling, concentrated positive region, which the model does not have.
s: Thomson's model allows only slight deflection
Bounce back needs concentrated positive charge

questions.q: Aarav says, 'Thomson's model was useless because a better model replaced it.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the picture, though later replaced, was the first genuine attempt to describe how the atom's positive and negative charges stay balanced. Early models, though not fully correct, show how science moves forward one step at a time.

questions.q: A clay ball standing for +12 units of charge has 10 beads of -1 each pressed into it. Show that it cannot represent a neutral atom, and give two ways to correct it.
questions.a: Net charge = +12 - 10 = +2, so it is not neutral. It can be corrected by adding 2 more beads (12 beads), or by changing the clay's charge to +10.

questions.q: The chapter's hint asks you to compare thin foil with thick foil. If the gold foil in the experiment is made thicker, predict the number of alpha particles scattered sharply and the number passing straight through, with a reason.
questions.a: More alpha particles will be sharply scattered and fewer will pass straight through. A thicker foil has more layers of atoms, so each alpha particle has a greater chance of coming near a nucleus.
s: Reason: more chance of meeting a nucleus

questions.q: Describe the gold foil experiment: (i) who carried it out and when, (ii) the set-up, (iii) what Thomson's model predicted, (iv) what was actually seen, (v) why the experiment is also called the alpha-ray scattering experiment.
questions.a: (i) Geiger and Marsden, under Rutherford, in 1911. (ii) A narrow beam of alpha particles aimed at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. (iii) The positive charge was spread evenly, so alpha particles should pass straight through or be deflected only slightly. (iv) Most passed through undeflected, some were sharply deflected, a few bounced back. (v) The deflection from the straight path is called scattering.

questions.q: Rohan sets up a glass tube with two electrodes at very low gas pressure and applies a high voltage. (i) What does he observe moving, and between which electrodes? (ii) He changes the cathode metal and the gas. What does he observe? (iii) What does he conclude about electrons? (iv) Which model of the atom does the discovery lead to? (v) What value of charge is taken as -1 by convention?
questions.a: (i) Rays (cathode rays) move from the cathode to the anode. (ii) The nature of the rays stays the same. (iii) Electrons are a fundamental component of all atoms, present in every element. (iv) Thomson's plum pudding model. (v) The charge of an electron, -1.602 x 10^-19 C, is taken as -1.
s: Rays unchanged by metal or gas

questions.q:
Neha makes a clay-and-bead model of a Thomson atom for her class in Surat. The clay is meant to carry +8 units of charge and each bead stands for -1 unit.
(a) How many beads make the model neutral?
(b) She has only 6 beads. What is the net charge of her model?
(c) She finds that a smear of paint on the clay carries -1 unit of charge, and she uses 8 beads. Does the model still represent a neutral atom?
(d) She can either remove one bead or scrape off the paint. Which fix keeps the model representing the atom with +8 units of positive charge, and why?
questions.a: (a) 8 beads. (b) +8 - 6 = +2, so the model is positively charged. (c) Net charge = +8 - 1 - 8 = -1, so it is not neutral. (d) Scrape off the paint: that restores +8 units of positive charge balanced by 8 beads; removing a bead gives +8 - 1 - 7 = 0 but then the model would stand for 7 electrons and a smaller positive charge, so it would not be the same atom.

questions.q:
A school simulation of the gold foil experiment fires 2000 alpha particles at a thin foil. The screen shows 1990 particles going straight through, 8 sharply deflected and 2 bounced back.
(a) What percentage of the particles were sharply deflected or bounced back?
(b) What does this small percentage suggest about the region that causes the deflections?
(c) Which feature of Thomson's model does the bounce back go against?
(d) To see more rare events in the same time, the class can use a thicker foil or fire more particles. Choose one and state a drawback.
questions.a: (a) (8 + 2)/2000 = 0.005, which is 0.5%. (b) The region is very small, so the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus. (c) Thomson's even spread of positive charge, which predicted only slight deflection. (d) A thicker foil gives each particle more chance of meeting a nucleus, but fewer particles then pass straight through, blurring the picture; firing more particles keeps the thin foil but takes longer. Either choice with a drawback.
s: Part (d): a choice with a drawback

questions.q: A school draws an atom to scale on a playground 150 m across, using the chapter's size ratio between atom and nucleus. About how wide should the nucleus be?
questions.a: The nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom: 150 m / 100000 = 0.0015 m = 1.5 mm.
o: 1.5 mm, about the size of a pepper grain
15 mm, about the width of a thumb
1.5 m, about the height of a child
0.15 mm, about the width of a hair

questions.q: A sheet of paper is 3 x 10^-4 m thick. Taking one atom to be about 10^-10 m across and stacking atoms one on another, about how many atoms make up its thickness?
questions.a: Number of atoms = 3 x 10^-4 / 10^-10 = 3 x 10^6, about thirty lakh atoms.

questions.q: In a gold foil trial one alpha particle comes straight back towards the source. Which statement best fits Rutherford's picture of the atom?
questions.a: Only a small, dense, positively charged nucleus can throw an alpha particle back; empty space or evenly spread charge cannot.
o: It met a dense, positively charged nucleus almost head-on
It collided with an electron that was heavier than it
It was absorbed by an evenly spread positive charge
It passed through empty space and was then pulled back

questions.q: Which statement about what the gold foil experiment showed is NOT correct?
questions.a: The experiment did not show neutrons; they were discovered later by Chadwick.
o: It showed that neutrons are present in the nucleus
It disproved the plum pudding model
Large deflections showed that charge and mass are packed into a tiny centre
Passing straight through showed that most of the atom is empty space

questions.q: The nucleus of a neutral atom carries a total positive charge of +16 units. What can be said about the atom?
questions.a: The nucleus charge comes from protons, each +1, so 16 protons; a neutral atom has equal electrons, so total charge is zero.
o: It has 16 protons and 16 electrons, and is electrically neutral
It has 16 protons and 8 electrons, and is neutral
It has 16 electrons and 16 neutrons, and is neutral
It has 16 protons and 16 electrons, and carries +16 charge

questions.q:
Read the statements about Rutherford's work.
Statement 1: The nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom.
Statement 2: Protons are much lighter than electrons.
Statement 3: Rutherford's model explained fully why atoms are stable.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Protons are much heavier than electrons, and the model could not explain stability, so only statement 1 is correct.
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Rutherford's model an electron orbiting the nucleus should lose energy.
Reason (R): A particle moving in a circular path keeps changing direction, so it is accelerating.
questions.a: Both are true: the accelerating electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: If an atom is magnified until it is 50 m across, its nucleus would be ___ mm wide.
True or False: Rutherford's model placed the electrons around the nucleus correctly, but it could not explain why atoms do not collapse. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. An electron going round in a circle is constantly accelerating and should lose energy, spiral in and fall into the nucleus, yet atoms are stable.
s: Reason: accelerating electron should lose energy and spiral in

questions.q:
An atom of an element has 19 protons in a neutral state.
(a) How many electrons does it have?
(b) Where are the 19 protons, and what share of the atom's mass lies there?
questions.a: (a) 19 electrons, equal to the protons. (b) In the nucleus, which holds most of the atom's mass.
s: Part (b): nucleus, most of the mass

questions.q:
A 400 m ground stands for an atom of diameter 10^-10 m, and the nucleus is 10^-15 m.
(a) By what factor is the nucleus smaller than the atom?
(b) What size of pepper grain stands for the nucleus on this ground?
A student says, 'Protons and electrons have equal and opposite charges, so they must have equal masses.' Correct her using the chapter.
questions.a: The charges are equal in size and opposite in sign, but protons are much heavier than electrons, so the masses are not equal.

questions.q: Why does the chapter bring in the idea that a circular path means acceleration when explaining the failure of Rutherford's model?
questions.a: A particle moving in a circle constantly changes direction, so it is accelerating. An accelerating electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.
s: Accelerating electron loses energy and spirals in

questions.q: Write the number of protons, electrons and the total positive and negative charge in units for a helium atom and for a sodium atom.
questions.a: Helium: 2 protons, 2 electrons, +2 and -2. Sodium: 11 protons, 11 electrons, +11 and -11. Both atoms are neutral.

questions.q: Priya says, 'A single alpha particle bouncing back is enough to rule out the plum pudding model.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. In Thomson's model the positive charge is spread evenly, so an alpha particle could be deflected only slightly. A sharp bounce back needs a small region of concentrated positive charge, so the plum pudding model cannot hold.
s: Plum pudding allows only slight deflection

questions.q: Show, using the chapter's argument, why matter around us could not stay intact if Rutherford's planetary model were the whole truth.
questions.a: An electron in a circular path is accelerating, so it should lose energy. Losing energy it should spiral into the positive nucleus. Then atoms would collapse and not exist, but atoms are stable, so the model must be incomplete.

questions.q: A sheet is 0.05 mm thick and one atom is about 10^-10 m across. Find how many atoms stacked one above another make up its thickness. Show the unit conversion.
questions.a: 0.05 mm = 5 x 10^-5 m. Number = 5 x 10^-5 / 10^-10 = 5 x 10^5, which is five lakh atoms.

questions.q: State three conclusions Rutherford drew from the gold foil experiment, give the observation behind each, then give the size ratio of nucleus to atom and one limitation of his model.
questions.a: Most of the atom is empty space: most alpha particles passed undeflected. The nucleus is dense and holds all the positive charge and most of the mass: a few were sharply deflected or bounced back. Electrons revolve around it like planets around the Sun. Nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom. Limitation: it could not explain stability of the atom.

questions.q: Compare Thomson's and Rutherford's models on: (i) where the positive charge is, (ii) where the mass is, (iii) how well each explained the gold foil results, (iv) the place of electrons, and (v) say which you would keep in a school exhibit and why.
questions.a: (i) Thomson: spread through the sphere; Rutherford: concentrated in a nucleus. (ii) Thomson: spread; Rutherford: mostly in the nucleus. (iii) Rutherford's explained the results better; Thomson's failed on large deflections. (iv) Thomson: embedded; Rutherford: revolving around the nucleus. (v) A reasoned choice, for example Rutherford's, as it fits the experiment, while noting its stability limit.

questions.q:
Lakshmi's school in Chennai marks a 120 m field as a sodium atom for an activity. Students stand in as its particles.
(a) How wide is the nucleus on this scale?
(b) How many students represent the protons and how many the electrons?
(c) Students playing electrons circle the centre without slowing. What does Rutherford's model say should happen to a real orbiting electron?
(d) The teacher can say that the walking shows how a real atom stays stable, or note it only shows the planetary picture. Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) 120 m / 10^5 = 1.2 mm. (b) 11 protons and 11 electrons. (c) It is accelerating, so it should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. (d) The second statement is accurate: the picture shows Rutherford's model, which cannot explain stability, so saying it shows stability would mislead.

questions.q:
A new element Q has 15 protons. A student claims: 'Q has 15 electrons, the protons sit in the nucleus, and the nucleus is as wide as the atom.' Another student measures a model atom of diameter 10^-10 m and a nucleus of 10^-15 m.
(a) How many electrons does a neutral Q atom have?
(b) Where are the protons located?
(c) Compare the nucleus size with the atom size.
(d) Which part of the first student's claim should be corrected, and how would you reword it?
questions.a: (a) 15 electrons. (b) In the nucleus at the centre. (c) The nucleus is 10^5 times smaller than the atom. (d) The last part is wrong; reword: the nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom.

questions.q: In a model atom the shell energies are K = 2, L = 5 and M = 9 units. An electron jumps from K to M. What does it do with energy, and how much?
questions.a: An electron changes shells by absorbing or releasing energy equal to the difference of the two levels: 9 - 2 = 7 units, absorbed since it moves outward.
o: It absorbs 7 units
It releases 7 units
It absorbs 9 units
It absorbs 4 units

questions.q: In the same model atom (K = 2, L = 5, M = 9 units) an electron releases 3 units of energy and lands in the K-shell. From which shell did it start?
questions.a: Energy before = 2 + 3 = 5 units, which is the L-shell. M would have needed to release 7 units.
o: L-shell
M-shell
K-shell
N-shell

questions.q: A nucleus holds 7 protons and 7 neutrons. Ignoring electrons, how many times heavier than a hydrogen atom (1 proton, no neutron) is this atom?
questions.a: Mass comes from protons and neutrons, each about equal: 7 + 7 = 14 against 1, so about 14 times.
o: About 14 times
About 7 times
About 8 times
About 2 times

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Bohr's model?
questions.a: Allowing any distance with continuous energy loss is the Rutherford difficulty that Bohr's fixed shells removed.
o: An electron can orbit at any distance and lose energy continuously
The K-shell has the least energy
Electrons revolve only in allowed shells, not in between
An electron in a fixed shell does not lose energy

questions.q: Pooja predicts that iron should have 26 protons and 26 neutrons because lighter atoms such as carbon have equal numbers. What does the chapter say about heavier atoms?
questions.a: As atoms get heavier, nuclei have many more neutrons than protons: iron 26 protons and 30 neutrons, uranium 92 protons and 146 neutrons.
o: They have many more neutrons than protons; iron has 26 protons and 30 neutrons
They have fewer neutrons than protons, so iron has 24
They have equal numbers always, so Pooja is right
They have no neutrons, only protons

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: An electron in a stationary state loses energy continuously.
Statement 2: Chadwick's neutron has a mass nearly equal to the proton's and no charge.
Statement 3: Neutrons are present in the nucleus of every atom, including hydrogen.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: In a stationary state the electron's energy stays constant, and hydrogen has no neutron, so only statement 2 is correct.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Adding neutrons to a nucleus changes the atomic number of the element.
Reason (R): A neutron carries no electrical charge.
questions.a: A is false: atomic number is the number of protons, which neutrons do not change. R is true: the neutron is neutral.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A nucleus with 6 protons and 6 neutrons has about ___ times the mass of a hydrogen atom, ignoring electrons.
True or False: The neutron was needed to explain why atoms are heavier than their protons alone, so even the hydrogen nucleus contains a neutron. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Neutrons are found in the nucleus of all atoms except hydrogen; the common hydrogen nucleus is a single proton, while helium's mass of about four times hydrogen needs two neutrons.
s: Correction: no neutron in hydrogen; helium has 2 protons and 2 neutrons

questions.q:
(a) Iron has 26 protons and 30 neutrons. Find its neutron-to-proton ratio to two decimals.
(b) Uranium has 92 protons and 146 neutrons. Find its ratio and say which is higher.
questions.a: (a) 30/26 = 1.15. (b) 146/92 = 1.59; uranium's ratio is higher, showing heavier atoms need more neutrons.

questions.q:
(a) State the relative charges of the electron, proton and neutron.
(b) Hence find the total charge on a nucleus of 8 protons and 8 neutrons.
questions.a: (a) Electron -1, proton +1, neutron 0. (b) 8 x (+1) + 8 x 0 = +8.

questions.q: A student says, 'Rutherford's and Bohr's models are the same since both have electrons orbiting a nucleus.' Is she right?
questions.a: Partly. Both have circular paths, but in Bohr's model electrons move only in fixed shells of definite energy without losing energy, which explains stability; Rutherford's could not.
s: Fixed shells with no energy loss is the difference

questions.q: Why can the mass of electrons be ignored when finding the mass of the helium atom? Support with the chapter's numbers.
questions.a: Electrons are so light that their mass can be ignored; helium's mass of about four times hydrogen's is accounted for by 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

questions.q: Bohr introduced stationary states as a postulate. Is it reasonable to accept a postulate in science? Give a reasoned answer.
questions.a: Yes, if it explains observations: the postulate explained atomic stability and many experimental observations, and models can be improved later. A reasoned opposite view is also acceptable.
s: Justification from what the postulate explained

questions.q: Imran says, 'An electron with slightly less energy than the L-shell can stay between the K and L shells.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. Electrons can revolve only in the allowed shells and not in between them. To change shells an electron must absorb or release exactly the energy difference between two levels.

questions.q: In a model atom K = 2 and L = 5 units. Show that an electron in K that absorbs 2 units cannot stay in any shell, and say what amount would take it to L.
questions.a: After absorbing 2 units it would have 4 units, between K (2) and L (5), but electrons cannot exist between shells. Absorbing 5 - 2 = 3 units takes it to L.

questions.q: Using helium and hydrogen, explain the puzzle the discovery of the neutron solved.
questions.a: Helium has 2 protons and hydrogen 1, yet helium is about 4 times as heavy, not double. Chadwick found the neutron with mass near the proton's and no charge, so helium's mass is 2 protons plus 2 neutrons.

questions.q: A model atom has K = 3, L = 7, M = 12 and N = 18 energy units. Find: (i) energy to take an electron from K to M, (ii) energy released when N falls to M, (iii) the final shell of an L electron that absorbs 5 units, (iv) whether L can absorb 6 units and stay, (v) the energy to go from K to N.

Describe the discovery of the neutron: (i) the puzzle, (ii) who and when, (iii) the properties, (iv) the neutron-proton pattern from light to heavy atoms with two examples, (v) why heavy nuclei need many neutrons.
questions.a: (i) Helium has two protons but about four times hydrogen's mass. (ii) James Chadwick, 1932. (iii) Mass nearly equal to proton, no charge. (iv) Carbon 6 and 6, iron 26 and 30, uranium 92 and 146. (v) Neutrons reduce repulsion between protons by increasing the distance and strengthen the nuclear force.

questions.q:
A quiz-setter uses a model atom with energies K = 3, L = 7, M = 12 and N = 18 units. A lab device can deliver energy in fixed packets.
(a) How much energy lifts an electron from K to M?
(b) An electron in N releases 6 units. Where does it land?
(c) An L electron absorbs 6 units. Can it stay there?
(d) Device X delivers 4, 5 or 6 units on request; Device Y delivers only 15 units. To lift a K electron to N, which would you choose, and what do you lose?
questions.a: (a) 12 - 3 = 9 units. (b) 18 - 6 = 12, the M-shell. (c) 7 + 6 = 13 lies between shells, so no. (d) Both reach N (4 + 5 + 6 = 15 or one 15). X can also stop at L or M, but needs three steps; Y is quick but reaches only N from K.

questions.q:
Four nuclei: carbon 6 protons, 6 neutrons; oxygen 8 and 8; iron 26 and 30; uranium 92 and 146. A student has to guess the neutrons in a heavy nucleus with 83 protons.
(a) Find neutrons minus protons for each nucleus.
(b) Find the neutron-to-proton ratio for iron and uranium to two decimals.
(c) Why do heavy nuclei need extra neutrons?
(d) The student guesses 83 neutrons. Judge the guess using the pattern.
questions.a: (a) 0, 0, 4, 54. (b) 1.15 and 1.59. (c) Neutrons reduce repulsion between protons and strengthen the nuclear force. (d) Unlikely; heavy atoms have many more neutrons than protons, so the number should be well above 83.

questions.q: A storeroom clerk writes labels for bottles of cobalt, aluminium, chlorine and calcium. Which set follows the IUPAC capitalisation norm?
questions.a: The first letter is capital and the second, if any, is small: Co, Al, Cl, Ca.
o: Co, Al, Cl, Ca
CO, AL, CL, CA
co, al, cl, ca
CO, Al, Cl, Ca

questions.q: Sunita guesses the symbols of sodium and potassium from the first two letters of their English names, writing So and Po. Why does her method fail?
questions.a: Some symbols come from Latin, Greek or German names rather than English: Na from natrium and K from kalium.
o: Their symbols Na and K come from the Latin names natrium and kalium
Symbols are always the first letter alone
IUPAC bans the letters S and P for elements
Their symbols come from German names

questions.q: A neutral atom has 19 protons and 20 neutrons. What are its atomic number and mass number?
questions.a: Atomic number = protons = 19; mass number = protons + neutrons = 39.
o: Atomic number 19, mass number 39
Atomic number 20, mass number 39
Atomic number 19, mass number 20
Atomic number 39, mass number 19

questions.q: Which statement about mass number is NOT correct?
questions.a: Mass number counts protons and neutrons, not electrons; electron mass is negligible.
o: It is the number of protons plus electrons
It is denoted by A
It counts the nucleons in the nucleus
It is written above the atomic number in the notation

questions.q: An atom is written with mass number 31 and atomic number 15 before its symbol, P. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does a neutral atom have?
questions.a: Protons = 15; neutrons = 31 - 15 = 16; electrons = 15.
o: 15 protons, 16 neutrons, 15 electrons
31 protons, 15 neutrons, 31 electrons
15 protons, 31 neutrons, 15 electrons
16 protons, 15 neutrons, 16 electrons

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: IUPAC approves the names and symbols of elements.
Statement 2: The symbols Cl and Zn use a letter other than the second letter of the name.
Statement 3: Carbon with 6 protons and 6 neutrons is written with 12 above and 6 below the symbol C.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three agree with the chapter.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dalton's symbols of 1803 were pictures, while Berzelius's of 1813 were letters from Latin names.
Reason (R): IUPAC now approves the names and symbols of elements.
questions.a: Both are true, but IUPAC approval does not explain how the two earlier systems differed.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: An atom has atomic number 13 and 14 neutrons, so its mass number is ___.

Match each atom in column I with its mass number in column II.
Column I: 1. 9 protons, 10 neutrons  2. 11 protons, 12 neutrons  3. 17 protons, 18 neutrons  4. 14 protons, 14 neutrons
Column II: a. 35  b. 28  c. 19  d. 23
questions.a: Mass number = protons + neutrons: 19, 23, 35 and 28.

questions.q: True or False: When a neutron is added to the nucleus of an atom, its atomic number increases by one. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Atomic number is the number of protons; adding a neutron raises only the mass number by one.
s: Correction: atomic number counts protons, neutron changes mass number

questions.q:
(a) Write the symbols of sodium and potassium and the Latin names they come from.
(b) Why do scientists use these symbols instead of names in their own languages?
questions.a: (a) Na from natrium; K from kalium. (b) Symbols are internationally recognised, so scientists worldwide communicate clearly regardless of language.

questions.q:
An atom has atomic number 15 and mass number 31.
(a) Find its neutrons.
(b) Write it in the standard notation.
questions.a: (a) 31 - 15 = 16. (b) Mass number 31 above and atomic number 15 below, before the symbol P.

questions.q: A student writes the symbols HG, cL and zN for mercury, chlorine and zinc. Correct them and state the norm broken.
questions.a: Hg, Cl, Zn. The first letter is capital and the second, if any, is lowercase.

questions.q: Rina says, 'Hydrogen has atomic number 1 and mass number 1.' Check using the table of mass numbers.
questions.a: Yes. Hydrogen has 1 proton and 0 neutrons, so atomic number 1 and mass number 1 + 0 = 1.

questions.q: Compare how Dalton in 1803 and Berzelius in 1813 represented elements.
questions.a: Dalton introduced pictorial symbols; Berzelius suggested alphabetic symbols derived from Latin names.

questions.q: Rahul says, 'Atomic number tells the element and the electrons of a neutral atom, and mass number also tells the electrons.' Is he correct?
questions.a: Partly. Atomic number identifies the element and equals the electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number is protons plus neutrons and does not give the number of electrons.

questions.q: Show that no atom can have atomic number 12 and mass number 10.
questions.a: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 10 - 12 = -2. A number of neutrons cannot be negative, so it is impossible.

questions.q: Find the missing values: (i) atomic number 9 with 10 neutrons: mass number; (ii) mass number 32 with 16 electrons: protons and neutrons; (iii) mass number 39 with 20 neutrons: atomic number.
questions.a: (i) 19. (ii) 16 protons and 32 - 16 = 16 neutrons. (iii) 39 - 20 = 19.

questions.q: A riddle: I have mass number 39 and 20 neutrons. Find (i) protons, (ii) electrons in a neutral atom, (iii) my symbol and its Latin name from the table, (iv) my notation, (v) why my symbol is K and not k.
questions.a: (i) 19. (ii) 19. (iii) K, from kalium (potassium). (iv) 39 above, 19 below, before K. (v) The first letter of a symbol is always capital.

questions.q: Write a short note on the history and rules of symbols: (i) Dalton 1803, (ii) Berzelius 1813, (iii) the role of IUPAC, (iv) two capitalisation or letter-choice norms with examples, (v) why a worldwide standard is needed.
questions.a: (i) Pictorial symbols. (ii) Alphabetic symbols from Latin names. (iii) IUPAC approves names and symbols. (iv) First letter capital, second lowercase (Al not AL); Cl, Zn use another letter. (v) Different symbols would cause confusion; common symbols let scientists communicate regardless of language.

questions.q:
A school lab in Nagpur has bottles labelled AL, Hg, cu, FE and Zn. A new bottle holds atoms with 12 protons and 12 neutrons.
(a) Which labels break the norms and how are they corrected?
(b) Hg comes from which word and language?
(c) Give the mass number of the new atoms and write the notation (element Mg).
(d) Labels can show the symbol only, or the symbol with the Latin name for Hg and Fe. Choose one and state a drawback.
questions.a: (a) AL, cu, FE: Al, Cu, Fe. (b) Hydrargyros, Greek. (c) 12 + 12 = 24, written 24 above and 12 below Mg. (d) Either: symbol only is short but pupils may not link Fe to ferrum; adding Latin names helps but crowds the label.

questions.q:
A table lists four atoms: P has 17 protons and 18 neutrons; Q has 17 protons and 20 neutrons; R has 18 protons and 22 neutrons; S has 19 protons and 21 neutrons.
(a) Find the mass number of each.
(b) Which two atoms are the same element, and what shows it?
(c) R and S have the same mass number. Are they the same element?
(d) The lab sorts boxes by mass number or by atomic number. Which is better for identifying the element, and what does it hide?
questions.a: (a) 35, 37, 40, 40. (b) P and Q, same atomic number 17. (c) No, atomic numbers 18 and 19 differ. (d) Atomic number identifies the element; sorting by it hides differences in mass number.
s: Part (d): atomic number, hides mass number

questions.q: An element has 13 electrons in its neutral atom. What are its electronic configuration and its valency?
questions.a: Shells fill K 2, L 8, then 3 in M. With fewer than four valence electrons it loses them, so valency 3.
o: K = 2, L = 8, M = 3; valency 3, by losing 3 electrons
K = 2, L = 8, M = 3; valency 5, by gaining 5 electrons
K = 2, L = 11; valency 3
K = 3, L = 8, M = 2; valency 2

questions.q: An atom with 16 electrons combines with hydrogen. Using the combining capacity idea, how many hydrogen atoms will one atom of it combine with?
questions.a: Configuration 2, 8, 6: it gains 2 electrons to complete the octet, so its valency is 2 and it combines with 2 hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: A lab shelf has atoms with 2, 9, 10 and 11 electrons. Which two are largely unreactive because of their outer shells?
questions.a: The atom with 2 electrons has a full K-shell and the one with 10 electrons has configuration 2, 8, an octet; 9 (2, 7) and 11 (2, 8, 1) are incomplete.
o: The atoms with 2 and 10 electrons
The atoms with 9 and 10 electrons
The atoms with 2 and 11 electrons
The atoms with 10 and 11 electrons

questions.q: Which of the following electron distributions is NOT allowed by the Bohr-Bury rules?
questions.a: The L-shell must be complete (8) before electrons enter the M-shell, so 2, 7, 2 is not allowed.

questions.q: A silicon atom has the configuration 2, 8, 4. What does the chapter's rule predict about its behaviour?
questions.a: With exactly four valence electrons it can neither lose nor gain easily, so it shares four electrons.
o: It shares four electrons, so its valency is 4
It gains four electrons, so its valency is 4
It loses four electrons, so its valency is 4
It does nothing as its outer shell is an octet

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The K, L and M shells can hold at most 2, 8 and 18 electrons.
Statement 2: Nitrogen, 2, 5, has a valency of 3.
Statement 3: An atom with six valence electrons tends to lose them to reach an octet.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Six valence electrons means gaining two to reach an octet, so statement 3 is false.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An atom with seven valence electrons tends to gain one electron.
Reason (R): Atoms with more than four valence electrons lose their valence electrons to complete the octet.
questions.a: A is true: seven valence electrons gain one to make eight. R is false: atoms with more than four tend to gain electrons.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A phosphorus atom has 15 electrons, so it must gain ___ electrons to complete its octet.

Match each atom, given by its number of electrons in column I, with what it does to complete its octet in column II.
Column I: 1. 7 electrons  2. 12 electrons  3. 14 electrons  4. 16 electrons
Column II: a. loses 2 electrons  b. gains 3 electrons  c. gains 2 electrons  d. shares 4 electrons
questions.a: 7 electrons: 2, 5 gains 3; 12: 2, 8, 2 loses 2; 14: 2, 8, 4 shares 4; 16: 2, 8, 6 gains 2.

questions.q: True or False: The valency of oxygen is 2 both by its electronic configuration and by the fact that in water one oxygen atom combines with two hydrogen atoms. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. Oxygen is 2, 6, so it gains two electrons to complete its octet; in H2O it combines with two hydrogen atoms, which gives the same combining capacity of 2.
s: Reason: configuration gives 2 and H2O shows 2

questions.q:
(a) Write the electronic configuration of the atom with atomic number 15.
(b) State its valence electrons and its valency.
questions.a: (a) 2, 8, 5. (b) 5 valence electrons; it gains 3 to complete the octet, so valency 3.

questions.q:
(a) Write the configuration of atom with 16 electrons.
(b) How many hydrogen atoms will one such atom combine with, and why?
questions.a: (a) 2, 8, 6. (b) 2, because it gains two electrons to reach the octet, so its combining capacity is 2.

questions.q: Two students write the configuration of sodium as 2, 8, 1 and 2, 7, 2. Which is correct and which rule does the other break?
questions.a: 2, 8, 1 is correct. 2, 7, 2 breaks the rule that the L-shell must be filled before the M-shell.

questions.q: Why is argon (2, 8, 8) largely unreactive while chlorine (2, 8, 7) is reactive?
questions.a: Argon has a complete octet in its valence shell, so it is stable; chlorine has seven valence electrons and needs one more to complete its octet.

questions.q: The M-shell can hold 2 x 3^2 electrons. Calculate this and explain why argon places only 8 in its M-shell.
questions.a: 2 x 3^2 = 18. The outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons, and argon's M-shell is its outermost shell.

questions.q: Meena says, 'Carbon, with four valence electrons, will easily lose all four to reach a stable octet.' Is she correct?
questions.a: No. Carbon (2, 4) has four valence electrons and cannot easily gain or lose them; it shares four electrons, so its valency is 4.
s: Four electrons cannot easily be lost or gained

questions.q: Show that no atom can have the configuration 2, 10.
questions.a: The L-shell holds at most 2 x 2^2 = 8 electrons, so 10 cannot be in it. The extra two would have to go to the M-shell after L has 8.

questions.q: Write the configuration of an atom from the first eighteen elements that loses 3 electrons, name it and give its valency.
questions.a: 2, 8, 3 (aluminium), valency 3; 2, 3 (boron) also fits.

questions.q: For atoms with atomic numbers 9, 11, 14 and 18, write the configuration and, for each, say whether it loses, gains, shares or is stable. Give valency where it applies.
questions.a: 9: 2, 7 gains 1, valency 1. 11: 2, 8, 1 loses 1, valency 1. 14: 2, 8, 4 shares 4, valency 4. 18: 2, 8, 8 octet, stable and largely unreactive.

questions.q: Explain the octet rule and valency using oxygen, sodium and carbon, and show how water supports the valency of oxygen.
questions.a: An octet (or 2 for helium) in the valence shell makes an atom stable. Sodium 2, 8, 1 loses 1: valency 1. Oxygen 2, 6 gains 2: valency 2. Carbon 2, 4 shares 4: valency 4. In H2O oxygen combines with two hydrogen atoms, so its combining capacity is 2.

questions.q:
A technician in a Jaipur lab has 50 magnesium atoms and 90 chlorine atoms. In MgCl2 one magnesium atom combines with two chlorine atoms.
(a) Write the configurations of magnesium (12 electrons) and chlorine (17 electrons).
(b) Give the valency of each.
(c) How many MgCl2 units can be formed, and which atoms are left over?
(d) She can buy 10 more chlorine atoms to use all the magnesium, or accept the leftover. Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) 2, 8, 2 and 2, 8, 7. (b) Magnesium 2, chlorine 1. (c) 90/2 = 45 units, with 50 - 45 = 5 magnesium atoms left. (d) Buying 10 uses all 50 Mg (needs 100 Cl); accepting leftover saves cost but wastes 5 Mg atoms.

questions.q:
Five atoms P, Q, R, S and T have 7, 8, 11, 14 and 17 electrons.
(a) Write the configuration of each.
(b) State which lose, gain or share electrons and the valency.
(c) Which atom pairs with R in a 1 : 1 ratio by combining capacity?
(d) R can combine with T, Q or P. Which gives the smallest number of atoms per unit, and what does the pairing with P need?
questions.a: (a) 2, 5; 2, 6; 2, 8, 1; 2, 8, 4; 2, 8, 7. (b) P gains 3 (3); Q gains 2 (2); R loses 1 (1); S shares 4 (4); T gains 1 (1). (c) T. (d) T gives 2 atoms; Q needs 2 R per Q (3 atoms); P needs 3 R per P (4 atoms).
s: Part (d): T smallest, P needs 3 R

questions.q: A hypothetical element has two isotopes: mass 10 u making up 20% and mass 11 u making up 80%. What is its weighted average atomic mass?
questions.a: (10 x 20/100) + (11 x 80/100) = 2 + 8.8 = 10.8 u; 10.5 is the simple mean, which ignores abundance.

questions.q: Atoms M (6 protons, 6 neutrons), N (6 protons, 8 neutrons), O (7 protons, 7 neutrons) and Q (8 protons, 8 neutrons) are tested. Which pair are isobars?
questions.a: N and O both have mass number 14 but different atomic numbers. M and N are isotopes.
o: N and O
M and N
O and Q
M and Q

questions.q: A lab has a mixture of protium and deuterium gas. A student proposes separating them by a chemical reaction. Why will this not work well, and what could work instead?
questions.a: Isotopes have the same electrons and configuration, so similar chemistry, but differ in physical properties like boiling and melting points.
o: Their chemical properties are the same, but physical properties such as boiling point differ
Their chemical properties differ, but their boiling points are the same
Both are the same in every property
They have different numbers of electrons

questions.q: Which statement about the three isotopes of carbon, 12, 13 and 14, is NOT true?
questions.a: All have six protons; they differ only in neutrons.
o: They have different numbers of protons
They each have six electrons
They differ in the number of neutrons
They have the same chemical properties

questions.q: A museum wants the age of an ancient artefact, and a hospital wants to treat thyroid cancer. Which isotopes does the chapter point to?
questions.a: Carbon-14 is used to determine age; iodine-131 treats goitre and thyroid cancer.
o: Carbon-14 for the artefact and iodine-131 for the thyroid
Cobalt-60 for the artefact and carbon-14 for the thyroid
Uranium-235 for the artefact and cobalt-60 for the thyroid
Iodine-131 for the artefact and uranium-235 for the thyroid

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Isotopes of an element have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Statement 2: Isotopes have different chemical properties because their neutrons differ.
Statement 3: A weighted average atomic mass need not be a whole number.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Isotopes share atomic number and have similar chemical properties; only statement 3 is true.
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The average atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 u and not 36 u.
Reason (R): The isotope with mass 35 u is more abundant, about 75%, than the one with mass 37 u, about 25%.
questions.a: Both are true and the abundance difference explains why the weighted average is nearer 35.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Calcium, potassium and argon each have mass number 40. The argon atom has atomic number 18, so it has ___ neutrons.

Match each situation in column I with the term in column II.
Column I: 1. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 atoms  2. Argon-40 and potassium-40 atoms  3. 35 u (75%) and 37 u (25%) giving 35.5 u  4. Iodine-131 given to a patient with goitre
Column II: a. isobars  b. isotopes  c. weighted average atomic mass  d. medical use of an isotope
questions.a: Same Z, different A are isotopes; same A, different Z are isobars; abundance-based mean is weighted; iodine-131 is a medical use.

questions.q: True or False: Since the average atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 u, a single chlorine atom with a mass of 35.5 u exists in nature. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Chlorine atoms are 35 u or 37 u; 35.5 u is the weighted average over a large number of atoms.
s: Correction: 35.5 u is an average over atoms

questions.q:
(a) How many neutrons do deuterium (mass number 2) and tritium (mass number 3) have, given each has 1 proton?
(b) How many electrons does each have, and why are their chemical properties alike?
questions.a: (a) Deuterium 1, tritium 2. (b) One electron each; same electronic configuration, so same chemical properties.

questions.q:
A hypothetical element Q has isotopes of 24 u (80%) and 26 u (20%).
(a) Find its weighted average atomic mass.
(b) How much does it differ from the simple average?
questions.a: (a) 24 x 0.8 + 26 x 0.2 = 19.2 + 5.2 = 24.4 u. (b) Simple average = 25 u, so the difference is 0.6 u.

questions.q: Of 4 lakh chlorine atoms, 3 lakh are mass 35 u and 1 lakh are 37 u. Show that the average mass of an atom is 35.5 u.
State two differences between isotopes and isobars, with one example of each.
questions.a: Isotopes have the same atomic number and different mass numbers (carbon-12, carbon-14); isobars have different atomic numbers and the same mass number (argon-40, potassium-40).

questions.q: Dalton said all atoms of an element are identical in mass. Is this claim fully right?
questions.a: Partly: atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but isotopes have different numbers of neutrons and hence different masses.

questions.q: Anil says, 'Carbon-14 will react differently with oxygen from carbon-12 because it has more neutrons.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. Isotopes have the same number of electrons and electronic configuration, so chemical properties are the same; they differ in physical properties.

questions.q: Show that two atoms with 17 protons each cannot be isobars of each other.
questions.a: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Both atoms have atomic number 17, so they are the same element, not isobars; they could only be isotopes.

questions.q: A hypothetical element has isotopes of 24 u (79%), 25 u (10%) and 26 u (11%). Find its weighted average atomic mass.
Give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons for protium, deuterium, tritium, carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, and explain why each set shares chemical properties.
questions.a: Protium 1, 0, 1; deuterium 1, 1, 1; tritium 1, 2, 1; C-12 6, 6, 6; C-13 6, 7, 6; C-14 6, 8, 6. Within each set electrons and configuration are the same, so chemical properties are alike.

questions.q: A hypothetical element Y has isotopes of 63 u (70%) and 65 u (30%) in 10 lakh atoms. Find: (i) atoms of each, (ii) weighted average, (iii) simple average, (iv) why the simple average is wrong, (v) whether any atom has the weighted mass.
questions.a: (i) 7 lakh and 3 lakh. (ii) 63 x 0.7 + 65 x 0.3 = 63.6 u. (iii) 64 u. (iv) It ignores abundance. (v) No, it is an average.

questions.q:
A state health department lists four isotopes: cobalt-60 (27 protons), iodine-131 (53 protons), carbon-14 (6 protons) and uranium-235 (92 protons).
(a) Find the number of neutrons in each.
(b) Match each to its use.
(c) Which shares its atomic number with carbon-12, and what are the two called?
(d) A district hospital can buy only cobalt-60 or iodine-131. Choose one and state what is lost.
questions.a: (a) 33, 78, 8, 143. (b) Cobalt-60 cancer radiotherapy; iodine-131 goitre/thyroid; carbon-14 dating; uranium-235 reactor fuel. (c) Carbon-14; isotopes. (d) Either: cobalt-60 treats cancer generally but not the thyroid specifically; iodine-131 treats goitre and thyroid cancer but not other cancers.

questions.q:
Calcium (atomic number 20), potassium (19) and argon (18) each have mass number 40.
(a) Find the neutrons in each.
(b) What are such atoms called?
(c) A student says they must behave identically because of the same mass number. What decides chemical behaviour?
(d) Evaluate his claim.
questions.a: (a) 20, 21, 22. (b) Isobars. (c) The number of valence electrons (electronic configuration). (d) Incorrect: they are different elements with different atomic numbers and electrons, so they behave differently.
